title.en: The Crime of the Fallen Leaf

art_context: a parable written in 1918: Ranum Nuzarget, an Indian yogi exiled from the abode of the Great Initiation into a huge European-Russian city of war and revolution, sits in a summer square garden, converses telepathically with his far-away teachers, foresees the death of a passer-by whose soul is dead, and — though forbidden to use his power on pain of destruction — turns aside a bomber aeroplane by will alone; a fallen maple leaf brings him forgiveness. The narrator's voice is elevated, theosophical (Initiation, incarnations, Nirvana, the Highest of the High), with long periodic sentences, a touch of Grin's irony and pseudo-scientific precision (a table of durations of the exercises). The answers of the Great Initiation are solemn, scriptural, set out line by line. Setting: a large Russian city in the summer of 1918 (unnamed): a square garden with sand paths and maple trees, crowds in motley clothes, six-storey houses, a church, a river, a great empty cobbled square, trams; a 1910s biplane.
